issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Amir, a 40-year-old paramedic, still remembers the smell of the hospital antiseptic that night. He had been on duty when the call came in—a motorcycle accident, high speed, multiple trauma. He recognized the jacket before he saw the face. It was his younger brother, Samir. The visible injuries were catastrophic, and despite Amir’s frantic efforts, Samir died on the gurney. In the months that followed, Amir found that certain moments would send him spiraling: the sight of any visible wound on a patient, the sudden antiseptic scent that hit him when walking into the ER, or even a passing mention of accident victims. Each of these triggers would yank him back into that full-sensory reliving—the sound of the sirens, the warmth of blood on his gloves, the crushing weight of his own helplessness. There were whole stretches of the event he could not retrieve, no matter how hard he tried, and that gap felt like proof that his mind had simply shut down when it mattered most.

The memory brought back the same terror, and Amir came to believe he had permanently changed for the worse. Because the memory returned with such visceral force, he began to see reminders of it everywhere — in the colour of a patient's jacket, in the sound of a distant siren, in the way a colleague's hands moved. He told himself he should have protected Samir, that he couldn’t rely on himself anymore. These negative appraisals gnawed at him constantly: every time a new shift began, he felt his failure pressing on his chest. The trauma, he was certain, had broken something essential in him. That belief made him more watchful, more inclined to scan rooms for danger, and he began choosing where to sit based on how protected he felt—always with his back to a wall, facing the door. His concentration faltered; he would lose his train of thought mid-sentence when a colleague’s hand brushed his shoulder, making him startle with alarm. Living in this state of constant alert, Amir had come to see his hypervigilance as the most damning evidence that the trauma had shattered something permanent in him.

To cope, Amir developed a pattern of avoidance. He started calling in sick to work more often, staying home rather than exposing himself to the visual injuries and hospital smells that tormented him. Yet each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way he drove to avoid the hospital's emergency bay was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened, etching the event deeper into his daily landscape. Yet when he did go in, he threw himself into overworking—taking every extra shift, staying late, running from one call to the next—keeping his mind so occupied that he didn’t have to think about the trauma. He tried hard to suppress the memories, but the more he pushed them away, the more they erupted unbidden. The suppression itself seemed to feed the memory gaps, and the terror on recall grew sharper each time. Overworking left him exhausted, and the exhaustion only reinforced his sense that he couldn’t rely on himself—that he was constantly running from something inside him.

The cycles interlocked. Triggers at work—a child with a bleeding laceration, the smell of disinfectant—would immediately spike his threat response, making him jumpy and hypervigilant for the rest of the shift. That heightened threat then pulled his mind back to the reliving, and the reliving deepened his conviction that he had failed. He began to interpret small things as signs that he would fail again: a pager going off, a glance from a supervisor. His negative appraisals fed the threat, and the threat made him more sensitive to triggers he might otherwise have ignored. The avoidance and overworking, meanwhile, kept him from ever processing the event; each time he suppressed a thought, the memory returned more vividly, and each memory reinforced his sense of permanent damage. Even his wife noticed he had become distant, pulling away from touch, always scanning the room during dinner. He couldn’t explain why he needed to sit with his back to the wall; it just felt necessary.

He finally came to therapy after his wife told him she couldn’t bear to see him so afraid. Amir admitted he was terrified that he would never be the man he used to be—that the trauma had left a wound that could not heal. He wanted to stop the cycle, but he didn’t know how.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not describe a direct causal relationship where the trauma memory causes Amir to perceive or experience triggers; the memory influences triggers only indirectly through negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not show that Amir's maladaptive strategies (avoidance, overworking, suppression) directly cause him to perceive triggers; the strategies affect memory and appraisals but not triggers directly.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
